clue.text: Car's upholstery and part of its wheel as described in Yorkshire

blocks.note: Yorkshire speech clips 'the' down to a bare t' — t'pub, t'match — so the article shrinks to one letter.
The outer hoop of a wheel, the part the tyre sits on.

explanation.walkthrough: The surface talks about a car from start to finish, and the accent is doing real work: written down, that dropped definite article is nothing but an apostrophe and a single consonant.
explanation.definitionFit: Trim is the motor trade's word for the fabric, carpet and panelling an interior is finished with, rather than anything that has been trimmed.

clue.text: Went rapidly downhill?

blocks.note: Read figuratively this is how a business, a career or someone's health is said to decline; read plainly it is simply moving at speed.
The setter means an actual slope, and the question mark is the nudge: on snow, going down one at speed is a winter sport with its own verb.

explanation.walkthrough: There is nothing to take apart here — the whole clue is one phrase read twice. The idiom about decline is cashed in for a real hillside, a sledge and a lot of snow.
explanation.definitionFit: Going downhill fast is idiom for decline, but taken at face value it describes travelling a snowy slope on a sledge, which the past tense here reports.

clue.text: Launches risible reductions

indicators.note: Something risible is laughable and not to be taken seriously, and letters nobody takes seriously will not stay in the order they were handed over in.

blocks.note: Ten letters handed over intact, which is exactly the length of the entry.

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a company launching laughable cuts, which is the sentence a solver wants to believe. Counting the last word first is what breaks it open.
explanation.definitionFit: To introduce a product or a policy is to launch it, putting it before the public for the first time — the same act in a plainer register.

clue.text: Musical number that may be promoted on the boards?

definitions.text: may be promoted on the boards
definitions.note: The definition describes the answer instead of naming it — a relative clause saying what sort of thing gets promoted when it reaches the far side of a board.

blocks.note: Chess is a stage musical, written by Tim Rice with the two men from Abba and set at a world championship.
A number is a single item in a programme — a song, or any short work a musician performs.

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves of the wordplay are musical and the definition is not. 'The boards' pulls you towards a theatre, where a show gets promoted, and away from the board where a pawn does.
explanation.definitionFit: A pawn reaching the far rank is promoted, and only something standing on a chequered board can be; 'the boards' is also the stage the surface wants.

clue.text: Just: that man, Rev Spooner says, in the Vatican

indicators.note: The Reverend Spooner was famous for trading the opening sounds of two words as he spoke, so naming him is the instruction to swap them.

blocks.note: Just here is the adverb meaning merely or only.
The pronoun a clue reaches for when it means a male person at a distance.
Say those two words with their opening sounds traded, S for H, and the pious result is what you write in.

explanation.walkthrough: Say the plain version first and it is a flat little phrase nobody would write for its own sake — only him. That flatness is the tell: Spooner clues hide behind awkward wording.
explanation.definitionFit: The papal jurisdiction governed from Vatican City carries this name, so in everyday usage the two point at the same institution.

clue.text: Stylised screen at back of play?

definitions.text: Stylised screen at back of play?

indicators.note: To stylise something is to depart from its natural form, and letters departing from their natural form are letters rearranged.
This points at the far end of the word after it, asking for the final letter and nothing else.

blocks.note: Six of the seven letters, handed over whole.
The final letter of the word, which the instruction in front of it asks for.

explanation.walkthrough: This is the rare clue where every word does both jobs at once. The trap is taking 'screen' for the definition — a screen at the back of a stage — when it is the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Painted flats standing behind the actors really are a stylised screen at the rear of a production, so the sentence works as a straight description too.

clue.text: Truant perhaps having issue following bit of Maths

indicators.note: It tells you the word for offspring comes after, so the school-subject word leads the assembly and the family word trails it.

blocks.note: A bit of maths set to be worked out is a problem, the word for one exercise in a textbook.
Issue in the legal sense means a person's offspring, as in 'died without issue'.

explanation.walkthrough: 'Issue' is the word to own: in wills and law reports it means offspring, and setters use it constantly. The classroom surface is a decoy built round the other half.
explanation.definitionFit: A truant is one instance of the wider category, a youngster whose behaviour is a constant difficulty, and 'perhaps' flags that the answer is the class not the example.

clue.text: Scoff at tablets swallowed

definitions.note: Both words are slang mass nouns for food, and the answer only exists in that plural-looking form, so a singular definition is the only kind available.

indicators.note: Something swallowed disappears inside whatever took it, so the short word goes within the letters on either side.

blocks.note: E is the standing crossword letter for the drug ecstasy, sold as tablets, so more than one of them is ES.
The word is used exactly as it stands, dropped inside the pair around it.

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is somebody sneering at a pill-popper. 'Tablets' is the giveaway: a single E is the standard abbreviation, and a plural of it makes a two-letter shell.
explanation.definitionFit: Scoff is British slang for food, and the answer is the same idea in a more American register — grub you sit down to, as in 'good eats'.

clue.text: Physical exercise - cutting: 'en garde' discharged?

indicators.note: A blade cutting into something ends up inside it, which is where the two-letter abbreviation lands.
A battery discharged is a battery emptied, and a word emptied keeps only the letters at each end.

blocks.note: The French phrase opens and closes with the same letter, and everything between the two is thrown away.
PE is the timetable abbreviation for physical education, the school lesson.

explanation.walkthrough: The clue never stops talking about fencing, which is why there is no separate definition to underline: the whole sentence is the picture, and the wordplay hides inside the French.
explanation.definitionFit: An epee is the fencing sword, so the clue works as a loose picture of the sport rather than a synonym: exercise with a blade, on the call 'en garde'.

clue.text: Objections: proof of payment returned

indicators.note: Something returned comes back the way it went, so on an across entry the letters are read from the right-hand end.

blocks.note: The counterfoil you keep when a ticket or a cheque is paid, and the thing you wave when someone asks whether you paid.

explanation.walkthrough: The colon does the joining, which makes the first word look like a heading rather than the definition. Turn the counterfoil round and four letters of grumbling fall out.
explanation.definitionFit: Each objection raised against a plan is one of these — 'no ifs, no buts' is the phrase — so the plural noun names a set of them.

clue.text: Fly down with Spirit

blocks.note: Feeling down is feeling blue — the colour has stood for low spirits for centuries.
British slang for nerve or courage: someone who loses their bottle has lost their nerve.

explanation.walkthrough: 'Spirit' looks like it wants a drink and the capital letter sells the idea, but the sense wanted is courage. Both halves come out of everyday idiom rather than any dictionary of insects.
explanation.definitionFit: The big metallic blowfly that blunders into kitchens carries this name, so the definition works as a category with the answer an instance of it.

clue.text: Iffy clue - 'Cord (9)' - not resolved

indicators.note: Something iffy is dubious and not to be trusted, and letters you cannot trust have not been left in the order printed.

blocks.note: Eight of the twelve letters come straight from these two words.
The numeral in the quoted mini-clue is spelled out as a word and joins the pool.

explanation.walkthrough: The clue quotes a little clue at itself, enumeration and all, and that bracketed figure is not decoration — you write the number out in letters before shuffling.
explanation.definitionFit: Accounts or differences left unreconciled are ones nobody has squared away, so the adjective means precisely still outstanding.

clue.text: Shift in public opinion having sound basis at first

indicators.note: It reorders the two halves, telling you the word for a basis leads and the one standing in front of it in the clue trails.

blocks.note: The grounds for a decision are the basis it rests on, and the word is plural in that sense.
Sound here is the adjective for good condition: of a person, being sound is being in health.

explanation.walkthrough: The trap is hearing 'sound' as a noise, which sends you looking for the wrong kind of word. It is the adjective, and the clue's last two words say which piece goes first.
explanation.definitionFit: A broad build-up of feeling among ordinary people takes this name from the deep ocean wave that rises far away from any storm.

clue.text: Rude, curt male nunnery reformed

indicators.note: A curt reply is one cut short, so the word standing behind it loses its final letter.
To re-form is to form again in a different arrangement, which is what a pool of letters does here.

blocks.note: The word arrives with its last letter already trimmed away by the adjective in front of it.
All seven letters join the pool, which is where the doubled N comes from.

explanation.walkthrough: Everyman's surface is a small joke about a religious house. The mechanism runs in two steps, and the second only comes out right once the first has thrown a letter away.
explanation.definitionFit: The older adjective for a person with no manners levels the same charge as rude, aimed squarely at behaviour rather than at speech.

clue.text: Alas! Escort lost in flights

indicators.note: Something lost has strayed from where it belongs, and letters that have strayed are no longer standing in their proper places.

blocks.note: The exclamation and the noun together supply exactly ten letters.

explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation mark is the disguise: 'Alas!' reads as the setter's aside rather than as fodder, so the letter count comes out four short until you count it in.
explanation.definitionFit: A flight is one unbroken run of stairs between landings; these are moving stairs, so the plural names them by that staircase sense.

clue.text: An inspiration? Yours truly? I could do with a laugh

definitions.text: I could do with a laugh

blocks.note: The indefinite article, taken in its single-letter form.
A muse is the classical source of a poet's inspiration, one of nine goddesses.
Yours truly is how a writer signs off when referring to himself.

explanation.walkthrough: Two question marks in a row look like the setter hedging his bets; they are just flagging loose definitions. The definition is the whole back half, and it is a sentence rather than a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: 'I could do with a laugh' is what somebody says to ask for entertaining, and the answer is that same request put as an instruction.

clue.text: The old group of chaps is group of Arabians

blocks.note: Ye is the archaic form of the definite article, as in 'Ye Olde Tea Shoppe'.
Chaps is the everyday British word for a group of blokes.
The verb is taken as two letters and used just as it stands.

explanation.walkthrough: The trick is that the verb in the middle joins nothing at all — it is fodder, which is why the sentence reads so oddly if you try to take it as a statement.
explanation.definitionFit: The people of Yemen, at the southern end of the Arabian peninsula, are Arabians in the geographical sense the definition uses.

clue.text: Everyman regarded, in report, as one unpleasant to behold

indicators.note: A report is a spoken account of something, so the clue wants these words heard aloud rather than read off the page.

blocks.note: The setter's pen name, and a setter writing about himself is I — one spoken letter with a longer spelling.
To have regarded something is to have looked at it, and that past tense sounds, in British English, exactly like a word for tender.

explanation.walkthrough: Everyman naming himself is a house signature, and here it is doing wordplay rather than decoration. Both halves have to be said out loud before they will spell anything.
explanation.definitionFit: A building or a mess so ugly that looking at it is a small punishment is exactly what 'unpleasant to behold' names.

clue.text: Bind some of Gwen's lavender

indicators.note: It asks for a part of what follows rather than the whole, and a part taken without rearranging is a run of consecutive letters.

blocks.note: Seven letters run consecutively through this phrase, straddling the apostrophe and the gap between the words.

explanation.walkthrough: A hidden word lives or dies by its surface, and a woman with a bunch of lavender is about as innocent as they come. The apostrophe is the join your eye slides straight over.
explanation.definitionFit: To bind a person is to put them under another's control, and the answer is that relation at its most absolute.

clue.text: Primarily ostentatious outcry heaping liberal and lavish admiration?

definitions.text: ostentatious outcry heaping liberal and lavish admiration?

indicators.note: It points at what comes first in each word after it, which across a run of seven words means seven opening letters.

blocks.clueFragment: ostentatious outcry heaping liberal and lavish admiration
blocks.note: Seven words in a row, each giving up the letter it starts with.

explanation.walkthrough: Even 'and' is pulling its weight, which is the tell: when a clue's small words look load-bearing, count the initials. Read straight, the same sentence is what the exclamation means.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is itself a showy cry of appreciation, so the words supplying the initials also describe, straight through, what saying it amounts to.

clue.text: Where butter is put is repeatedly lucky

blocks.note: The literal reading: a bread roll, buttered.
The gambler's idiom for a run of good fortune that keeps going.

explanation.walkthrough: The two readings sit next to each other with only a verb between them, so the whole thing looks like a single statement. Split it after 'put' and both halves stand up on their own.
explanation.definitionFit: Butter goes on a bread roll, and someone on a roll is enjoying an unbroken run of luck — one phrase covering a plate and a winning streak.

clue.text: Estimate price of a Chardonnay, peut-être, one in resort

blocks.note: To cost a job is to work out what it will come to, and the indefinite article follows to round the chunk off.
Peut-être is French for perhaps, flagging Chardonnay as one example of a vin blanc, a white wine.
A stands for one, the way 'a dozen' means a single dozen.

explanation.walkthrough: Everyman likes a foreign holiday, and two languages are working at once: the French flags an example, and the Spanish that comes out of it means the white coast.
explanation.definitionFit: The stretch of Spanish Mediterranean coast around Benidorm and Alicante is holiday towns end to end, which makes it a resort in the broad sense.

clue.text: Rod's European

blocks.note: The plain object: a long thin length of wood or metal.
Read as a nationality rather than the adjective for the continent — a native of one particular country in the east of it.

explanation.walkthrough: 'Rod's' reads as a man's name with a possessive, and that is the whole disguise; it is really 'rod is'. Only one of the two definitions takes a capital letter.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is a long slender rod; the other, with a capital letter, is a native of Poland — four letters covering a stick and a nationality.

clue.text: Athletic events set back with lack of energy - and evidence of injury

indicators.note: Set back means put the other way round, so the letters of the word before it are read from its far end.
It marks what is missing, so the letter named next comes out of the assembly instead of joining it.

blocks.note: Races on a track are the athletic events, and five letters is one more than the entry has room for.
E is the physicist's symbol for energy, and the crossword's standard single letter for it.

explanation.walkthrough: 'Lack of energy' is a two-part instruction rather than a mood: the word has to be turned into its single letter before it can be taken away. The dashes are surface punctuation only.
explanation.definitionFit: The mark left behind where a wound has healed stands as lasting proof that the injury happened at all.

clue.text: Clip from radio's Cilla, to remember one that's Swinging

indicators.note: A clip is a short piece cut whole out of a longer recording, so take an unbroken run out of what follows.

blocks.note: Ten letters in an unbroken run across three words, an apostrophe and a comma.

explanation.walkthrough: Cilla Black was a Liverpool singer who became one of British television's biggest hosts, so the surface is pure nostalgia — and the punctuation between the words is what hides the run.
explanation.definitionFit: An oscillator is the circuit that produces a steadily alternating signal, moving back and forth between two values, which is swinging in the engineer's sense.

clue.text: After change of heart, writer showing élan

indicators.note: The heart of a word is its middle, and changing it here means turning that central pair round rather than replacing them.

blocks.note: A Biro is the everyday British name for a ballpoint pen, after its Hungarian inventor Laszlo Biro.

explanation.walkthrough: 'After' is doing nothing but holding the sentence upright. The convention worth keeping is the pen, which turns up constantly as a four-letter writer, and here only its middle moves.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are borrowed words for dash and vigour in performance, one taken from French and one from Italian, and they name the same spirited energy.

clue.text: Erased 'sea lions' at first - rewritten as: ___

indicators.note: It asks for the opening letter only of the word it follows, which is why just one letter of that word joins the pool.
Rewriting is setting the same characters down again in a new arrangement, which is the instruction to reorder them.

blocks.note: Six letters straight off the first word of the clue.
The first of the two quoted words in full, then only the opening letter of the second.

explanation.walkthrough: The blank at the end is where the answer goes, and the joke is that the quoted phrase does double duty: it defines the answer and supplies most of its letters at once.
explanation.definitionFit: Sea lions belong to the family with visible ear flaps, so the definition names the answer by one of its members rather than by a synonym.

clue.text: Grasses grow, you hear?

indicators.note: It says the definition is met by sound and not by spelling, so say the other word aloud and write down what reaches your ear.

blocks.note: To grow is to rise, and rise said aloud matches a plural word for a cereal grass.

explanation.walkthrough: Four words with nothing to spare: one is the definition, one is the sound, and the question mark flags that you are being asked to hear rather than to read.
explanation.definitionFit: Rye is a cereal grass grown for bread and for whisky, so the plural noun names crops or varieties of that grass.
